subject: Tyska
title: Word order and subordinate clauses
sourceSummary: The verb's position in main and subordinate clauses, and the conjunctions weil and dass.

questions.prompt: Where does the conjugated verb go in a German main clause?
questions.opener: This is almost always true, regardless of what comes first in the sentence.
questions.explanation: The conjugated verb goes in position two in a main clause: "Ich spiele Fußball" or "Heute spiele ich Fußball" — the verb is always the second element, regardless of what comes first.

questions.prompt: Choose the right word order: "Today I play football."
questions.opener: If the sentence starts with "heute", where does the verb go?
questions.explanation: "Heute" takes position one, but the verb still has to go in position two: "Heute spiele ich Fußball." The subject "ich" moves after the verb.

questions.prompt: Where does the conjugated verb go in a subordinate clause introduced by "weil" (because)?
questions.opener: Subordinate clauses break the position-two rule.
choices: At the end of the clause
questions.explanation: In subordinate clauses introduced by weil, dass, wenn, and others, the conjugated verb is sent to the end of the clause.

questions.prompt: Choose the right sentence: "I'm staying home because I'm sick."
questions.opener: The verb "bin" should go at the end of the clause after "weil".
choices: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich bin krank.
Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich krank bin.
Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil bin ich krank.
Ich bleibe, weil zu Hause ich krank bin.
questions.explanation: "Weil ich krank bin" — the verb "bin" goes at the end of the clause.

questions.opener: A very common conjunction for introducing a subordinate clause.
questions.explanation: "Dass" means "that", as in "Ich weiß, dass du recht hast" (I know that you're right). Just like "weil", "dass" sends the conjugated verb to the end of the clause.

questions.prompt: Write the German conjunction that means "because"/"since" and sends the verb to the end of the clause.
Correct the error: "Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich möchte nach Berlin reisen."
questions.opener: The verb "möchte" should move to the end of the clause.
questions.answer: Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich nach Berlin reisen möchte.
steps: After "weil", the conjugated verb ("möchte") should stand at the end of the clause, not directly after the subject.
"Weil ich möchte nach Berlin reisen" → "weil ich nach Berlin reisen möchte".
Full sentence: "Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich nach Berlin reisen möchte." (I'm learning German because I want to travel to Berlin.)

questions.prompt: How does word order work in main clauses compared to subordinate clauses in German?
questions.opener: One of the clearest differences between German and Swedish.
questions.answer: Main clause: the conjugated verb always stands in position two, regardless of what comes first (Ich spiele heute. / Heute spiele ich.). Subordinate clause (after weil, dass, wenn, ob, and others): the conjugated verb moves to the LAST position in the clause (..., weil ich krank bin. / Ich weiß, dass du recht hast.). Common subordinate-clause conjunctions: weil = because, dass = that, wenn = if/when, ob = whether.

questions.prompt: Which element ALWAYS stands in position two in a German main clause?
questions.opener: This holds regardless of what comes first in the sentence.
questions.explanation: The conjugated verb always stands in position two in a main clause, no matter what comes first.

questions.prompt: Choose the right word order: "On Saturdays I play football."
questions.opener: The sentence starts with the time expression "am Samstag".
questions.explanation: "Am Samstag" takes position one, but the verb "spiele" still has to go in position two: "Am Samstag spiele ich Fußball."

questions.opener: A common conjunction for a condition or a point in time.
questions.explanation: "Wenn" means "if"/"when" and introduces a subordinate clause where the verb moves to the end.

questions.opener: Often used after expressions like "I don't know...".
questions.explanation: "Ob" means "whether", e.g. "Ich weiß nicht, ob er kommt" (I don't know whether he's coming).

questions.prompt: Choose the right sentence: "I think that he's right."
questions.opener: The verb "hat" should go at the end of the clause after "dass".
choices: Ich glaube, dass er recht hat.
Ich glaube, dass er hat recht.
Ich glaube, er dass recht hat.
Ich glaube, dass recht er hat.
questions.explanation: "Dass er recht hat" — the verb "hat" goes at the end of the clause.

questions.prompt: Which sentence has the correct word order?
questions.opener: The verb "kommt" should stand at the end of the clause after "ob".
choices: Ich weiß nicht, ob er morgen kommt.
Ich weiß nicht, ob er kommt morgen.
Ich weiß nicht, ob kommt er morgen.
Ich weiß nicht, er ob morgen kommt.
questions.explanation: "Ob er morgen kommt" — the verb "kommt" goes at the end of the clause.

questions.prompt: If a subordinate clause (e.g. a weil-clause) comes FIRST in a whole sentence, e.g. "Weil ich krank bin, bleibe ich zu Hause" — what happens to the main clause that follows?
questions.opener: The entire subordinate clause counts as position one in the combined sentence.
choices: The main clause's verb comes right after the comma
The main clause's verb comes at the very end of the whole sentence
The subordinate clause must always come last
There's no difference compared to when the subordinate clause comes last
questions.explanation: The entire subordinate clause ("weil ich krank bin") counts as position one, so the main clause's conjugated verb ("bleibe") comes right after the comma, in position two.
